passage: Rain had flooded the lane, so Jahnavi ran for the school bus with no time for breakfast. By second period the maths teacher was drawing pizza slices on the board to explain fractions, and all Jahnavi could think about was real pizza. Then the smell of samosas frying in the canteen drifted in. Her stomach growled so loudly that Rafiq looked up. When the teacher asked her what three-quarters meant, she had no answer at all; she hadn't heard a word. At recess Rafiq split his paratha with her. After that, back at her desk, the pizza slices finally made sense, and she asked Rafiq to show her the part she'd missed.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi have no time for breakfast?
qa.a: Rain had flooded the lane, so she ran for the school bus with no time for breakfast.

qa.q: What was on Jahnavi's mind during the fractions lesson?
qa.a: She kept thinking about real food, like pizza and the frying samosas, so hunger crowded out the lesson and she felt lost when asked a question.

qa.q: What smart choice did Jahnavi make after recess?
qa.a: Once she had eaten, she asked Rafiq to show her the part she had missed, so she could catch up instead of staying lost.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see Jahnavi's blank answer in class?
qa.a: Rafiq heard her stomach growl, so he probably understood she was hungry rather than careless, which is why he shared his paratha.

grounding: A child who skipped breakfast can think only of food and misses a lesson, and can follow it again after eating.

qa.q: What was the turning point that could stop this happening again?
qa.a: Darshan told his mother honestly that hunger stopped him learning, and they put bananas by the door so he can eat even on night-shift mornings.

qa.q: How was the lab lesson for Madhav?

passage:
I'm Arohi, and last Friday I learned something about my brain. Kamal Bhaiya took ages in the bathroom, so I, his little sister, had no time for breakfast and ran to the bus with an empty stomach.
In history, Ma'am was telling us about old trade routes and camels carrying spices. Usually I love that stuff. But all I could think about was Mummy's aloo paratha. My stomach growled so loudly the boy next to me laughed. When Ma'am asked me a question, I hadn't even heard it. I felt so silly.
At break I ate two bananas and my friend's poha. In the afternoon, history made sense again. Now I keep a biscuit packet in my bag.

qa.q: What did Arohi eat at break?
qa.a: Two bananas and her friend's poha.

qa.q: Why did Arohi feel silly when Ma'am asked her a question?
qa.a: She hadn't even heard it because her mind was stuck on food, even though she usually loves history.

qa.q: What choice did Arohi make after that day, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: She keeps a biscuit packet in her bag, so a missed breakfast won't take over her mind in class again.

qa.q: How might Ma'am have seen Arohi when she didn't answer?
qa.a: Ma'am might have thought Arohi wasn't paying attention, not knowing she was too hungry to follow the lesson.

grounding: It shows a schoolchild who came without breakfast and could think only of food, missing a lesson she normally enjoys.

passage:
Class 4 note, Tuesday. Ira Sen, class teacher.
During reading circle, Aadhya lost her place three times and asked me twice, "Ma'am, when is lunch?" She is usually the first to put up her hand. Today she stared at the clock. When I bent down, she whispered, "My tummy is making noises. I can't think." Her mother is travelling this week and her father leaves early for work, so she had come without breakfast.
I took her to the staff room and gave her a packet of biscuits and water. Twenty minutes later she read her paragraph aloud and asked a question about the story.
Next: I will message her father today and tell him about the school's breakfast corner for early arrivals.

qa.q: What did Aadhya whisper to Ira Sen?
qa.a: My tummy is making noises. I can't think.

qa.q: How can you tell Aadhya's mind was on food rather than the story?
qa.a: She kept losing her place, stared at the clock and asked twice when lunch was, though she is usually eager to answer.

qa.q: Which of Ira Sen's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Giving Aadhya biscuits and water right away helped most, because once her hunger eased she could read aloud and even ask about the story.

qa.q: How might Aadhya's father feel when he gets the message?
qa.a: He may feel a little guilty that she went hungry, and relieved to learn about the breakfast corner for busy mornings.

grounding: It shows a schoolchild who came without breakfast and could only think of food, unable to follow reading until she had eaten.

passage:
Harsha's mother had been on the night shift at the hospital, so there was no breakfast that morning in their Nagpur flat. Harsha, nine, drank a glass of water and went to school.
In science, Vidya ma'am was talking about the solar system. Harsha loved planets. But today every word slid away. He could only think of the smell of the canteen samosas, the biscuits in Chintu's bag, the time till break: forty minutes.
He wrote "Jupiter" in his notebook and then drew a paratha next to it.
Vidya ma'am noticed. After class she asked him quietly, "Did you eat today?"
He shook his head.
She gave him a banana from her desk and sat with him while he ate. Then she drew Saturn's rings for him again, slowly.

qa.q: How long was it till break?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling during the science class?
qa.a: He felt hungry and distracted, unable to enjoy even his favourite topic because food filled his thoughts.

qa.q: How did Vidya ma'am help, and what could she do next?
qa.a: She asked quietly, gave him a banana and re-explained Saturn; next she could check with his family about breakfast on night-shift days.

qa.q: How might Harsha's mother feel if she knew?
qa.a: She might feel worried and sorry, and want to find a way for him to have breakfast on her night-shift days.

grounding: It shows a schoolchild who came without breakfast unable to follow a lesson he loves as his mind narrows to food.

passage:
"Charu. Charu!" Nandini whispered.
"What?"
"Do you have anything to eat?"
"We're in the middle of history."
"I didn't have breakfast. I overslept."
"Just wait for break."
"I can't. All I can think about is food. Sir said something about a king, and all I heard was 'kheer'."
Charu snorted. "Seriously?"
"Seriously. I've read this page three times. I don't know what's on it."
"Nandini, what did I just say?" Sir asked.
Nandini froze. "Um… a king?"
At break, Charu pushed her lunchbox across. "Eat my idli. Then read the page again."
Nandini did. "Oh," she said. "It's about the canal. That's actually interesting."

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling during history class?
qa.a: Nandini felt hungry, scattered and frustrated, unable to focus because food filled every thought.

qa.q: What helped Nandini, and what could she try next time?
qa.a: Eating Charu's idli helped Nandini focus; next time Nandini could keep a snack handy or tell the teacher about missing breakfast.

qa.q: How does Charu see Nandini's problem at first, and then?
qa.a: At first Charu finds it funny and says to wait, but then shares the idli and sees how much it helps.

At lunch I ate everything. Then maths suddenly made sense again when Rafiq showed me his notes. It was strange, like my brain had been closed while I was hungry.
Now I keep a banana in my bag, just in case.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 3B

During the morning English lesson, Aditi, usually quick to answer, stared out of the window and kept looking at the tiffin shelf. She asked twice what time the break was. When Swati asked her for the eraser, she did not hear.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was the worst maths test day because I didn't eat breakfast. The gas cylinder ran out and Amma said we'd eat after school. I, Lavanya, sat in the test and the numbers kept floating. I read question three about four times. All I could think of was Deepika's lunch box. It smelled of lemon rice.
My hand was shaky and I felt so annoyed at everything. I left two questions blank that I KNOW how to do.
At break Deepika gave me half her lemon rice without me asking. After that I felt normal again and did my English work easily.
Tomorrow I'm going to tell Miss about the test. Maybe she'll understand.

qa.q: Why didn't Lavanya eat breakfast?
qa.a: The gas cylinder ran out and Amma said they'd eat after school.

qa.q: How was Lavanya feeling during the maths test?
qa.a: Lavanya felt shaky and annoyed at everything, with a mind stuck on food, so the numbers kept floating.

qa.q: What would you advise Lavanya to say to Miss tomorrow?
qa.a: To explain honestly that there was no breakfast that day and hunger made it hard to think, and ask if there's a way to show those two answers.

qa.q: How might Deepika have felt sharing her lemon rice?
qa.a: Deepika probably felt kind and caring, noticing her friend was hungry without being asked.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child who skipped breakfast able to think only of food during a test until eating at break.
